input.text: [lane-plover] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to a server that has moved or been retired, so pages fail or load wrongly. (2) Slow recovery: when a site switches to a backup server during an outage, cached answers delay the switch for many users. (3) Lingering bad answers: a forged or mistaken record stays in the cache longer, so harm lasts longer before it expires.

input.text: [lane-plover] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier, version 7, which starts with a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) Larger keys: it takes 16 bytes, against 4 or 8 for a normal integer, so indexes and foreign keys grow and fewer entries fit in memory. (2) Leaked timing: because the creation time is built into the value, anyone who sees an identifier can work out roughly when the row was made. Ordering is also only approximate between servers whose clocks differ, though it still inserts far more smoothly than random UUIDv4.

input.text: [lane-plover] A lease-based lock gives one holder the lock for a set time, and each machine decides for itself when that time is up using its own clock. If one clock runs fast or slow, the holder may think it still has the lock while the lock service thinks it has expired and hands it to someone else. Two holders then act at once, which the lock was meant to prevent. How large the skew must be to cause this is unknown.

Clock skew breaks lease-based locks because each machine uses its own clock to decide when a lease has run out.

A lease gives one holder the lock for a set time. If the holder's clock runs slow, or the lock service's clock runs fast, the holder may think it still has the lock after the service has given it to someone else. Two holders then act at once, which is what the lock was meant to prevent. I wrote "unknown" for how much skew it takes to cause this, since no figure was given.
